implementation_notes: All Swift structs are value types: assignment and argument passing copy, mutation requires a `var` binding plus a `mutating` method, and the compiler synthesises `==`/`hashValue` when the type declares `Equatable`/`Hashable` and all stored properties conform. That is the value-object structure as the language default, with identity (`===`) reserved for class instances - exactly the reference/value split the pattern draws; a class-based value type survives only for Objective-C/`NSObject` interop.
pitfalls: Synthesised `==`/`hashValue` include every stored property, so adding a cache or derived stored property changes equality - keep derived values computed.
A struct containing reference-type members (class instances, closures) compares those members by reference, so equality is only as deep as the members allow.
Public `var` properties let any holder mutate the value; expose `let` properties and `mutating` methods (or replace the whole value) so the conceptual whole stays consistent.
